entries.label: adjective, noun
entries.meaning: As an adjective, possible in the future but not yet real (*a potential problem*). As a noun, qualities or abilities that could develop and lead to success.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in the news and in everyday talk. The adjective almost always comes before a noun (*potential buyers*, *a potential risk*). The noun is usually uncountable: *have potential*, *a lot of potential*, *reach your full potential*, and *the potential for* + noun means the possibility of something.
entries.pattern: a potential + buyer / risk / problem; have (a lot of) potential; the potential for + noun
examples: We've had three **potential** buyers look at the house, but no offers yet.
The coach says my son has real **potential** as a goalkeeper.
Doctors are warning about the **potential** risks of taking the two drugs together.

drill.sentence: The old farmhouse needs a new roof, but with some work it has a lot of {{potential}}.
drill.hint: noun: possibilities for future success (not *promise*)

entries.related: *possible* — can happen, more general; *promise* — signs of future success (*shows promise*); *prospective* — expected to become something (*prospective students*).

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To start dealing with a problem, task or situation in a particular way or from a particular angle.
entries.usage: Common at work, in teaching and in advice: *approach a problem from a different angle*, *approach the conversation carefully*. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition, while the noun takes *to* (*a new approach to the problem*). The same verb also means come nearer to a place or person.
entries.pattern: approach + a problem / task / topic + carefully / differently / from an angle
examples: If you **approach** the conversation calmly, your landlord is more likely to listen.
Every surgeon **approaches** this operation a little differently.
I used to **approach** debugging without a plan; now I start from the last version that worked.

drill.sentence: When my daughter refuses to do her homework, I try to {{approach}} it with humor instead of yelling.
drill.hint: one verb for taking on a problem in a particular way (not *handle*, *tackle*, *address* or *deal with*)

mistake.wrong: We need to approach to this problem differently.
mistake.right: We need to approach this problem differently.
mistake.why: The verb *approach* takes a direct object; only the noun is followed by *to* (*an approach to the problem*).

entries.related: *tackle* — deal with a hard problem actively; *handle* — deal with, more general; *address* — formal, start dealing with an issue.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: As a result of what was just said; therefore. It can also mean *in this way*.
entries.usage: Mainly in academic, legal and formal writing, where it links a cause to its result; in conversation it sounds stiff, so people say *so* or *that's why*. It often comes before an *-ing* form (*…, thus reducing costs*) or after *and* or a semicolon. *Thus far* means *so far* and is also formal.
entries.pattern: …, thus + -ing; and thus …; thus far
examples: Prices rose much faster than wages, **thus** making it harder for young people to buy a home.
The new filter removes most of the noise, **thus** making the signal easier to detect.
She was the only candidate with hospital experience and was **thus** the obvious choice.

drill.sentence: This recipe uses brown butter instead of regular butter, {{thus}} giving the cookies a nutty flavor.
drill.hint: formal adverb meaning *as a result* (not *thereby* or *hence*)

entries.related: *therefore* — formal, introduces a logical conclusion; *hence* — formal, often before a noun phrase (*hence the delay*); *thereby* — by doing this, before *-ing*.

entries.label: adverb, adjective
entries.meaning: Considering everything together; in general, or in total.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing. As an adverb it often starts a sentence to give a general judgment (*Overall, the trip was great*) or follows a ranking (*third overall*). As an adjective it goes before a noun: *the overall cost*, *the overall winner*, *my overall impression*.
entries.pattern: Overall, …; the overall + cost / effect / impression / winner
examples: There were a few delays, but **overall** the move went smoothly.
The **overall** cost of the wedding came to about thirty thousand dollars.
Our team finished third **overall** in the regional tournament.

drill.sentence: The hotel room was small and the breakfast was cold, but {{overall}}, we really enjoyed the trip.
drill.hint: one word: taking everything into account (not *generally* or *basically*)

mistake.wrong: I looked overall for my keys.
mistake.right: I looked everywhere for my keys.
mistake.why: *Overall* means *in general* or *in total*; it never means *everywhere* like German *überall*.

entries.related: *on the whole* — very close, a little more formal; *all in all* — used to sum up; *in total* — only for amounts.

entries.label: adjective, preposition
entries.meaning: *Prior* means earlier, or existing before something (*prior experience*); *prior to* means *before*.
entries.usage: *Prior to* is common in official notices, legal, medical and business writing (*Do not eat prior to surgery*); in conversation, *before* sounds more natural. The adjective goes before a noun: *prior experience*, *prior knowledge*, *a prior commitment*. After *prior to*, use a noun or *-ing*, not a full clause.
entries.pattern: prior to + noun / -ing; prior + experience / knowledge / commitment
examples: Patients should not eat or drink anything for eight hours **prior to** surgery.
No **prior** experience is necessary; we'll train you on the job.
I'd love to come, but I have a **prior** commitment that evening.

drill.sentence: All passengers must check in at least two hours {{prior to}} departure.
drill.hint: a formal two-word way to say *before* (not *ahead of*)

mistake.wrong: Please call us prior to you arrive.
mistake.right: Please call us before you arrive. / Please call us prior to arriving.
mistake.why: *Prior to* is followed by a noun or *-ing*; before a full clause, use *before*.

entries.related: *previous* — the one before (*my previous job*); *preceding* — coming just before, formal; *subsequent to* — formal for *after*.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To need something, or to make something necessary, often because of a rule or the nature of a task; more formal than *need*.
entries.usage: Common in rules, job ads, instructions and formal writing: *The job requires a driver's license*, *Passengers are required to wear seat belts*. Typical patterns are *require* + noun, *be required to do*, and *require someone to do*. In conversation, *need* or *have to* sounds more natural, and *I require coffee* sounds comically formal.
entries.pattern: require + noun; be required to + verb; require someone to + verb
examples: Most rental companies **require** a credit card, not a debit card.
All visitors are **required** to sign in at the front desk.
Training a model this size **requires** thousands of GPU hours.

drill.sentence: In this state, all drivers are {{required}} to carry proof of insurance in the car.
drill.hint: past participle: made necessary by law (not *obligated*, *obliged* or *supposed*)

entries.related: *need* — everyday word; *demand* — require strongly, often a lot of effort (*the job demands patience*); *call for* — make necessary, less formal.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Happening at the beginning of a process or event; first.
entries.usage: Common at work, in medicine and in the news: *initial results*, *my initial reaction*, *the initial cost*. It goes before the noun and often suggests that things changed or may change later. The adverb *initially* means *at first*.
entries.pattern: initial + reaction / results / cost / plan / stages
examples: My **initial** reaction was to say no, but the offer grew on me.
The **initial** cost of solar panels is high, but they save money over time.
**Initial** results from the trial look promising, but the sample is small.

drill.sentence: Her {{initial}} plan was to stay in Chicago for a year, but she ended up living there for twenty.
drill.hint: adjective: at the very beginning (not *original* or *first*)

entries.related: *original* — the first one, before changes; *preliminary* — coming before the main part, formal; *final* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The largest amount that something can hold, produce or deal with; also a person's ability to do or feel something.
entries.usage: Common in business, engineering, health and the news: *a stadium with a capacity of 60,000*, *the hospital is at capacity*, *operate at full capacity*. With people, *the capacity for* + noun or *the capacity to* + verb means ability (*a capacity for hard work*). *In my capacity as …* is a formal way to say *in my role as …*.
entries.pattern: a capacity of + number; at (full) capacity; the capacity to + verb / for + noun
examples: The concert hall has a **capacity** of two thousand, and every seat was sold.
The ER was at full **capacity**, so ambulances were sent to other hospitals.
Kids have an amazing **capacity** to adapt to a new country.

drill.sentence: The new battery has twice the {{capacity}} of the old one, so the phone lasts two full days.
drill.hint: noun: how much energy it can hold (not *power* or *size*)

mistake.wrong: Professor Lang is a real capacity in heart surgery.
mistake.right: Professor Lang is a leading expert in heart surgery.
mistake.why: German *Kapazität* can mean an expert; English *capacity* never describes a person this way.

entries.related: *capability* — the ability to do something, often technical; *volume* — the amount of space inside; *overcapacity* — more than is needed.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make certain that something happens or is the case.
entries.usage: Common in work emails, policies, instructions and formal writing: *Please ensure that all doors are locked*. It is followed by a *that*-clause or a noun (*ensure safety*). Don't confuse it with *assure* (tell someone something to remove their doubt) and *insure* (protect with insurance), though some Americans also write *insure* for *ensure*.
entries.pattern: ensure (that) + clause; ensure + safety / quality / success
examples: Please **ensure** that your phone is turned off during the exam.
Lifeguards are on duty to **ensure** the safety of swimmers.
We added automated tests to **ensure** the fix doesn't break anything else.

drill.sentence: The school hired two extra crossing guards to {{ensure}} that the kids get across the busy road safely.
drill.hint: one verb: make certain (not *guarantee* or *make sure*)

mistake.wrong: I ensure you the package will arrive tomorrow.
mistake.right: I assure you the package will arrive tomorrow.
mistake.why: You *assure* a person to remove their doubt; you *ensure* that something happens.

entries.related: *make sure* — everyday equivalent; *guarantee* — promise firmly; *safeguard* — protect from harm.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Compared with other things or with what is normal; fairly or quite (*relatively easy*, *relatively cheap*).
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing before adjectives and adverbs: *relatively small*, *relatively quickly*, *relatively new*. It makes a claim more careful, because it admits that the judgment depends on a comparison. *Relatively speaking* is a common spoken phrase.
entries.pattern: relatively + adjective / adverb; relatively few / little
examples: The apartment is **relatively** cheap for this part of Boston.
Cataract surgery is now a **relatively** quick procedure, and most patients go home the same day.
The restaurant is **relatively** new, so there aren't many reviews yet.

drill.sentence: For a big city, Minneapolis has {{relatively}} little traffic, so my commute is easy.
drill.hint: adverb: when compared with other cities (not *comparatively* or *fairly*)

entries.related: *comparatively* — very close, more formal; *fairly* — to some degree, no comparison implied; *extremely* — much stronger.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To keep saying firmly that something is true, especially when other people doubt or deny it.
entries.usage: Common in news reports, legal contexts and formal writing: *He has always maintained his innocence*, *She maintains that she was never told*. It takes a *that*-clause or *innocence*, and it signals that the claim is disputed, so reporters use it to stay neutral. In conversation people say *keep saying* or *insist*.
entries.pattern: maintain (that) + clause; maintain your innocence
examples: He has always **maintained** his innocence, and his lawyers are asking for a new trial.
My grandmother **maintains** that a spoonful of honey cures any cold.
The company **maintains** that the recall was voluntary, not forced by regulators.

drill.sentence: Despite the video, the player still {{maintains}} that he never touched the referee.
drill.hint: one verb: he keeps saying it is true, despite doubts (not *insists*, *claims* or *swears*)

entries.related: *insist* — say firmly, often with emotion; *claim* — say something that may not be true; *assert* — state confidently, formal.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The income that a company receives from sales, or that a government receives from taxes, before costs are subtracted.
entries.usage: Common in business, finance and the news: *annual revenue*, *revenue grew by ten percent*, *tax revenue*, *generate revenue*. It is different from *profit*, which is what is left after costs. It is usually uncountable, but *revenues* is also used, especially in finance writing.
entries.pattern: annual / tax / ad revenue; generate / bring in revenue; revenue from + source
examples: The bakery's **revenue** doubled after it started selling online, but so did its costs.
Tourism is the island's main source of **revenue**.
The city expects higher sales tax **revenue** this year because of the new mall.

drill.sentence: The festival brought in a million dollars in ticket {{revenue}}, but after paying the bands, it barely made a profit.
drill.hint: noun: income before costs (not *sales*)

entries.related: *profit* — what is left after costs; *income* — money received, also by people; *turnover* — British for a company's total sales.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Mostly, or to a great extent, but not completely.
entries.usage: Common in news, academic writing and careful speech, often before a cause or a past participle: *largely due to*, *largely responsible for*, *largely ignored*. It shows that something is mostly true but leaves room for exceptions, so it sounds careful. *Mostly* is more conversational.
entries.pattern: largely + due to / because of / responsible for / ignored / unchanged
examples: The delay was **largely** due to bad weather in Chicago.
The neighborhood is **largely** residential, with only a few small shops.
Her warnings were **largely** ignored, and the project went over budget.

drill.sentence: The town's economy depends {{largely}} on tourism, so a rainy summer hurts everyone.
drill.hint: adverb: to a great extent but not completely (not *mainly*, *mostly*, *heavily* or *primarily*)

entries.related: *mainly* — very close, more neutral; *mostly* — conversational; *entirely* — completely, with no exceptions.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To change in position, direction, focus or attitude, or to make something change in this way.
entries.usage: Very common in the news, business and everyday speech: *shift the focus to*, *shift the blame onto*, *opinion has shifted*, *shift your weight*. It often suggests a gradual or partial move rather than a complete change. It works with or without an object, often with *from … to …* or *toward*.
entries.pattern: shift (something) from A to B / toward B; shift the blame onto someone
examples: During the pandemic, many companies **shifted** their meetings online.
Stop trying to **shift** the blame onto your brother; you broke the vase.
Public opinion on the new stadium has **shifted** since the costs were published.

drill.sentence: As she got older, her interests {{shifted}} from team sports to hiking and climbing.
drill.hint: past-tense verb for a gradual change of focus (not *changed*, *moved* or *turned*)

entries.related: *change* — more general; *move* — physical or general; *a shift* — the noun, also a period of work (*the night shift*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Correct and exact in every detail, without mistakes.
entries.usage: Common in science, journalism and everyday talk about information, measurements, descriptions and tools: *accurate data*, *an accurate description*, *the forecast was accurate*. *Accurate* means correct; *precise* means exact and detailed, and a precise measurement can still be inaccurate. *Pretty accurate* is common in speech.
entries.pattern: an accurate + description / picture / forecast / measurement; 100 percent accurate
examples: The witness gave the police an **accurate** description of the car, down to the dent in the bumper.
Is this map **accurate**? The road it shows doesn't seem to exist.
The new test gives **accurate** results in under ten minutes.

drill.sentence: Make sure the address on the form is {{accurate}}, or your package will end up at the wrong house.
drill.hint: adjective: free of mistakes (not *correct* or *right*)

mistake.wrong: My roommate is very accurate; his desk is always perfectly tidy.
mistake.right: My roommate is very neat; his desk is always perfectly tidy.
mistake.why: *Accurate* means correct or exact, not tidy like German *akkurat*; for people, say *neat*, *meticulous* or *careful*.

entries.related: *precise* — exact and detailed; *correct* — without errors, more general; *inaccurate* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In the end, after a long process; or at the most basic level, when everything is considered.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing, usually at the start of a sentence or before the main verb: *Ultimately, it's your decision*. It often signals the final or most important point after a discussion of details. *Eventually* stresses that something happened after a long time; *ultimately* stresses the final result or the basic truth.
entries.pattern: Ultimately, …; ultimately + verb (decide / depend / lead to)
examples: We looked at a dozen houses, but **ultimately** we decided to keep renting.
**Ultimately**, the success of any diet depends on whether you can stick to it.
The surgery was risky, but it **ultimately** saved his life.

drill.sentence: Your parents can give you advice, but {{ultimately}}, you're the one who has to live with the choice.
drill.hint: adverb: when everything is considered (not *in the end* or *finally*)

entries.related: *eventually* — after a long time or delay; *in the end* — conversational; *at the end of the day* — informal, used to state the basic point.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A particular way of thinking about something, shaped by your experience or position; a point of view.
entries.usage: Common in discussion, writing and the media: *from my perspective*, *a fresh perspective*, *a different perspective on*. *Put something in perspective* means compare it with other things to see how important it really is. Use *on* for the topic: *her perspective on remote work*.
entries.pattern: from someone's perspective; a (fresh / different) perspective on + topic; put something in perspective
examples: From a parent's **perspective**, the new school schedule is a nightmare.
Living abroad for a year gave me a whole new **perspective** on my own country.
The novel tells the whole story from the family dog's **perspective**, and it's surprisingly moving.

drill.sentence: It helps to talk to someone outside the company; they can offer a fresh {{perspective}} on the problem.
drill.hint: noun: a new way of seeing it (not *view*, *angle* or *take*)

entries.related: *point of view* — very close, more conversational; *viewpoint* — similar; *outlook* — general attitude toward life or the future.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A law or a set of laws passed by a lawmaking body such as Congress or a state legislature.
entries.usage: Common in the news, law and business: *pass*, *introduce* or *propose legislation*, *new legislation on* + topic. It is uncountable, so say *a piece of legislation* or *a law*. In conversation, people usually just say *a law* or *a bill*.
entries.pattern: pass / introduce / propose legislation; legislation on + topic; a piece of legislation
examples: The state passed new **legislation** requiring helmets for all e-scooter riders.
Small businesses often complain that new **legislation** creates too much paperwork.
Under the new **legislation**, landlords must give tenants sixty days' notice before raising the rent.

drill.sentence: Congress is considering {{legislation}} that would require airlines to refund passengers for long delays.
drill.hint: uncountable noun: proposed laws (not *a bill*)

mistake.wrong: The state passed a new legislation on e-bikes.
mistake.right: The state passed new legislation on e-bikes. / The state passed a new law on e-bikes.
mistake.why: *Legislation* is uncountable, so it takes no *a*; for one law, say *a law* or *a piece of legislation*.

entries.related: *a bill* — a proposed law before it passes; *regulation* — a rule made by a government agency; *legislature* — the body that makes laws.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: To some degree, but not very much; slightly.
entries.usage: Common in writing and careful speech before adjectives, comparatives and verbs: *somewhat better*, *somewhat surprised*, *it has improved somewhat*. It sounds a little more formal than *kind of* or *a bit* and is useful for understatement. *Somewhat of a* + noun is common, though some editors prefer *something of a*.
entries.pattern: somewhat + adjective / comparative; verb + somewhat
examples: The second season was **somewhat** better than the first, but I still didn't finish it.
I was **somewhat** surprised that she didn't come to the wedding.
Prices have dropped **somewhat** since the summer, so it may be a good time to buy.

drill.sentence: The new medication helped {{somewhat}}, but she still had headaches most mornings.
drill.hint: adverb: to a limited degree (not *slightly*, *some*, *a bit* or *a little*)

entries.related: *slightly* — a small amount; *rather* — fairly, often surprising; *considerably* — much more strongly.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: By a large or important amount, enough to make a real difference.
entries.usage: Common in the news, business and academic writing: *significantly higher*, *significantly reduce*, *differ significantly*. In research papers it usually means *statistically significant*, so careful writers avoid it there unless they ran a test. In speech, *a lot* or *much* is more natural.
entries.pattern: significantly + comparative / reduce / increase / improve
examples: Rents in our neighborhood have gone up **significantly** over the last two years.
Regular exercise can **significantly** reduce the risk of heart disease.
The new version of the app is **significantly** faster, especially with large files.

drill.sentence: After the new highway opened, traffic on our street dropped {{significantly}}, and the kids can play outside again.
drill.hint: adverb: by a large, noticeable amount (not *sharply*, *dramatically*, *considerably* or *substantially*)

entries.related: *considerably* — very close, without the statistics sense; *substantially* — by a large amount, formal; *slightly* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Final, coming at the end of a long process; or the greatest, best or most extreme of its kind.
entries.usage: Common in the news, writing and advertising: *the ultimate goal*, *the ultimate responsibility*, *the ultimate decision*. In marketing and casual speech it means *the best possible* (*the ultimate road trip*). It almost always goes before a noun, usually with *the* or a possessive.
entries.pattern: the / our ultimate + goal / aim / responsibility / decision; the ultimate + noun (best)
examples: Our **ultimate** goal is to open a clinic in every county in the state.
The **ultimate** decision rests with the parents, not the school.
For my brother, a week of fishing in Alaska is the **ultimate** vacation.

drill.sentence: Saving money is nice, but our {{ultimate}} goal is to buy a house before the kids start school.
drill.hint: adjective: the one at the very end, the most important (not *main*, *final* or *real*)

entries.related: *final* — last in a series; *eventual* — happening in the end, not necessarily the most important; *main* — most important, with no sense of an end point.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Large in amount, area or range; covering many details or a wide area.
entries.usage: Common in formal and work contexts: *extensive experience*, *extensive damage*, *extensive research*, *an extensive collection*. It sounds more formal than *a lot of* or *big*, and it is frequent in job ads, news reports and reviews. The adverb is *extensively* (*travel extensively*).
entries.pattern: extensive + experience / damage / research / knowledge / collection
examples: The fire did **extensive** damage to the kitchen, so we've been eating takeout for a month.
She has **extensive** experience in pediatric nursing, so we hired her right away.
The library has an **extensive** collection of old maps of the city.

drill.sentence: The hotel offers an {{extensive}} breakfast buffet, with everything from fresh fruit to made-to-order omelets.
drill.hint: adjective: wide-ranging, with many items (not *impressive*, *enormous* or *elaborate*)

entries.related: *comprehensive* — complete, including everything needed; *thorough* — careful and detailed; *limited* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Always behaving or performing in the same way; or, of ideas and statements, not contradicting each other.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports, parenting and research: *consistent results*, *a consistent player*, *be consistent with your kids*. *Consistent with* means *in agreement with* (*The injuries are consistent with a fall*). The noun is *consistency*.
entries.pattern: be consistent (in / about something); consistent with + fact / evidence
examples: She's not the fastest runner on the team, but she's the most **consistent**.
The pizza at that place isn't amazing, but it's **consistent**: it tastes exactly the same every time.
His story isn't **consistent** with what the security camera shows.

drill.sentence: The doctor said the bruises on her arm were {{consistent}} with a fall from a bike.
drill.hint: adjective: in agreement with, matching (not *compatible*)

mistake.wrong: You have to be consequent with your kids.
mistake.right: You have to be consistent with your kids.
mistake.why: German *konsequent* is *consistent* in English; *consequent* means *resulting* and is rare.

entries.related: *reliable* — can be trusted to do what is expected; *steady* — not changing suddenly; *inconsistent* — the opposite.

entries.label: adverb, preposition
entries.meaning: Without being affected or influenced by something; *regardless of* + noun means *whatever the situation with* that thing.
entries.usage: Common in speech and writing: *regardless of age*, *regardless of the cost*, *regardless of whether …*. *Regardless* alone at the end of a clause means *anyway* (*It was raining, but we went regardless*). *Irregardless* is heard in speech but is widely seen as nonstandard, so avoid it.
entries.pattern: regardless of + noun / wh-clause / whether …; … regardless (= anyway)
examples: The museum is free for all visitors, **regardless of** age.
**Regardless of** what the forecast says, pack a raincoat; it's Seattle.
We told him the trip was too expensive, but he booked it **regardless**.

drill.sentence: The gym charges the same monthly fee {{regardless of}} how often you go.
drill.hint: two words: the fee is not affected by it (not *no matter* or *irrespective of*)

entries.related: *no matter* — conversational (*no matter how often*); *irrespective of* — formal; *despite* — even though something exists.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Mainly; for the most part, more than for any other reason or purpose.
entries.usage: Common in writing and formal speech: *primarily because*, *primarily used for*, *primarily responsible for*. It names the most important part while allowing others. Americans stress the second syllable; many British speakers stress the first.
entries.pattern: primarily + because / for / used for / responsible for
examples: The store sells **primarily** organic produce, but it carries a few regular brands too.
I moved to Denver **primarily** for the job, but the mountains were a nice bonus.
The clinic **primarily** treats sports injuries.

drill.sentence: This rule exists {{primarily}} to protect young children, not to annoy parents.
drill.hint: adverb: more than for any other purpose (not *mainly*, *mostly*, *chiefly* or *largely*)

entries.related: *mainly* — very close, more conversational; *chiefly* — similar, slightly formal; *partly* — only to some extent.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The basic systems and structures that a country, city or organization needs to function, such as roads, bridges, power, water and networks.
entries.usage: Common in the news, politics, business and tech: *invest in infrastructure*, *aging infrastructure*, *public infrastructure*. It is usually uncountable. In tech, it also means the servers, networks and software that a service runs on.
entries.pattern: invest in / repair / upgrade infrastructure; aging / public / digital infrastructure
examples: Many American cities are struggling to repair aging **infrastructure** like bridges and water pipes.
The town's **infrastructure** couldn't handle the flood, and half the roads washed away.
Our **infrastructure** team keeps the servers running at night and on weekends.

drill.sentence: Before the Olympics, the city spent billions on {{infrastructure}}: new subway lines, roads and a bigger airport.
drill.hint: noun: basic public systems (not *construction* or *projects*)

entries.related: *facilities* — buildings and equipment for a purpose; *utilities* — power, water and gas services; *public works* — construction projects paid for by the government.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The process or period of changing from one state, situation or system to another.
entries.usage: Common at work, in health, education and the news: *the transition from school to work*, *a smooth transition*, *the transition to electric cars*. It suggests a process that takes time and needs managing. In American business English it is also a verb (*transition to a new role*).
entries.pattern: the transition from A to B; a smooth / difficult transition; in transition
examples: The **transition** from high school to college was harder than I expected.
The bank promised a smooth **transition** for customers moving to the new app.
Many retirees find the **transition** to a life without work surprisingly difficult.

drill.sentence: Moving from a big city to a small farm town was a huge {{transition}} for our kids.
drill.hint: noun: the process of moving from one way of life to another (not *change*, *adjustment* or *shift*)

entries.related: *change* — more general; *shift* — a move in direction or focus; *adjustment* — getting used to something new.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In the same order as the items just mentioned, so that the first matches the first, the second matches the second, and so on.
entries.usage: Mainly in writing: reports, papers, news and formal emails (*Anna and Ben are eight and eleven, respectively*). It usually comes at the end of the sentence after a comma. Don't confuse it with *respectfully*, which means politely.
entries.pattern: A and B + verb + X and Y, respectively
examples: The first and second prizes went to Lisa and Omar, **respectively**.
My sons, Leo and Max, are seven and ten, **respectively**.
The two models reached 81 and 85 percent accuracy, **respectively**.

drill.sentence: At the café, a large coffee and a pot of tea cost four and six dollars, {{respectively}}.
drill.hint: adverb: in the order just given

mistake.wrong: We can meet on Monday respectively Tuesday.
mistake.right: We can meet on Monday or Tuesday.
mistake.why: *Respectively* only matches two lists in order; it does not mean *or* or *or rather*, like German *beziehungsweise*.

entries.related: *respectfully* — politely, with respect; *in that order* — conversational equivalent; *each* — for one-to-one matching in speech.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: In the most important ways, ignoring small details; basically.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing to simplify or summarize: *It's essentially the same phone*, *Essentially, they want more money*. It signals *I'm simplifying, but this is the main point*. In writing it sounds more careful than *basically*, which can sound like a filler.
entries.pattern: essentially the same / + adjective; Essentially, …
examples: The new phone is **essentially** the old one with a better camera.
**Essentially**, the landlord wants us out by June.
The two drugs work in **essentially** the same way, but one is much cheaper.

drill.sentence: The ending of the movie is confusing, but {{essentially}}, the whole story was the main character's dream.
drill.hint: adverb: in its most important sense (not *basically* or *in essence*)

entries.related: *basically* — conversational, can be a filler; *in essence* — formal; *fundamentally* — at the deepest level.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To get something, especially through effort, a request or an official process.
entries.usage: Common in formal writing, official and legal texts and research: *obtain a permit*, *obtain permission*, *obtain a visa*. In conversation, *get* is much more natural, and *obtain* can sound bureaucratic. It is often passive: *Information was obtained from …*.
entries.pattern: obtain + a permit / permission / a visa / a copy / consent
examples: You'll need to **obtain** a permit before you build a deck.
The reporter **obtained** a copy of the letter from a former employee.
Written consent was **obtained** from all participants before the interviews.

drill.sentence: Foreign students must {{obtain}} a visa before they can enroll in the program.
drill.hint: formal verb: come to have it through an official process (not *get*, *secure*, *receive* or *acquire*)

entries.related: *get* — everyday word; *acquire* — come to own or learn something, formal; *secure* — get something hard to get (*secure funding*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Happening or coming after something else.
entries.usage: Common in formal writing, the news, law and medicine: *in subsequent years*, *subsequent studies*, *the subsequent investigation*. It goes before a noun, and the adverb *subsequently* means *later* or *afterward*. In conversation, *later* or *next* is more natural.
entries.pattern: subsequent + years / events / visits / doses; subsequently
examples: The first season was a hit, but **subsequent** seasons lost viewers.
He was arrested in March, and the **subsequent** trial lasted six months.
Any **subsequent** changes to your reservation will cost an extra fifty dollars.

drill.sentence: She was diagnosed in May and spent the {{subsequent}} months in and out of the hospital.
drill.hint: formal adjective: coming after that (not *following*, *next* or *later*)

entries.related: *following* — next, often *the following day*; *previous* — the opposite; *consequent* — resulting from something, rare.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A story or account of events, or a particular way of explaining events that reflects a point of view.
entries.usage: Common in literature, journalism, politics and business: *a compelling narrative*, *the official narrative*, *change* or *control the narrative*. In the second sense it often suggests that the explanation is shaped on purpose, so it can sound skeptical. As an adjective, *narrative* describes storytelling (*a narrative poem*).
entries.pattern: a compelling / dominant / official narrative; change / control the narrative
examples: The **narrative** jumps back and forth between 1940s Paris and present-day New York.
The official **narrative** is that the CEO left to spend more time with his family.
The museum's new exhibit presents a more honest **narrative** of the city's history.

drill.sentence: The team lost ten games in a row, and the new owner wants to change the {{narrative}} before ticket sales drop.
drill.hint: noun: the way people explain what is happening (not *story*, *mood*, *perception* or *conversation*)

entries.related: *story* — more general and conversational; *account* — a report of events; *spin* — a biased way of presenting events, critical.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on good reasons or evidence, so it deserves to be taken seriously; or officially acceptable and still in effect, like a ticket or passport.
entries.usage: Common in discussion and official contexts: *a valid point*, *a valid concern*; *a valid passport*, *valid for thirty days*. *That's a valid point* is a polite way to accept part of someone's argument. The opposite is *invalid*.
entries.pattern: a valid point / concern / argument; valid for / until + time; a valid ID / passport
examples: That's a **valid** point; I hadn't thought about the cost of parking.
Your passport must be **valid** for at least six months after you arrive.
The coupon is only **valid** on weekdays.

drill.sentence: Your worry about the cost is {{valid}}, but the cheaper option would break down within a year.
drill.hint: adjective: based on good reasons (not *fair*, *legitimate*, *reasonable* or *understandable*)

entries.related: *legitimate* — fair and acceptable, or legal; *sound* — based on good judgment (*sound advice*); *expired* — no longer valid.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Absolutely necessary or extremely important for something to succeed or exist.
entries.usage: Common in the news, health, work and formal speech: *vital information*, *play a vital role in*, *it is vital that …*. It is stronger than *important* and close to *essential* or *crucial*. In medicine, *vital signs* are pulse, breathing rate, temperature and blood pressure.
entries.pattern: vital to / for something; play a vital role in; it is vital that / to …
examples: Clean water is **vital** to a child's health.
Volunteers play a **vital** role in running the food bank.
It's **vital** that you take the full course of antibiotics, even if you feel better.

drill.sentence: In a power outage, a battery radio can be {{vital}} for getting news and emergency updates.
drill.hint: adjective: absolutely necessary (not *essential*, *crucial*, *critical* or *invaluable*)

entries.related: *essential* — necessary, very close; *crucial* — decisive for success; *vital signs* — basic body measurements.

entries.label: noun (plural)
entries.meaning: The results or conclusions of research, an investigation or an official inquiry.
entries.usage: Common in research, journalism, medicine and law: *the main findings*, *publish* or *present findings*, *the findings suggest that …*. It is usually plural; *a finding* is one specific result. In law, *a finding* is a formal decision about the facts.
entries.pattern: the (main / key) findings of + study / investigation; findings suggest / show that …
examples: The **findings** suggest that teenagers who sleep more do better in math.
The investigation's **findings** were released to the public on Monday.
The doctor walked us through the **findings** of my dad's MRI.

drill.sentence: The safety board will publish its {{findings}} on the train crash later this year.
drill.hint: noun: what the investigation discovered (not *report*, *results* or *conclusions*)

entries.related: *results* — more general; *conclusions* — what you decide from the results; *evidence* — facts that support a claim.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: More and more, as time passes.
entries.usage: Very common in the news, writing and speech, before adjectives and verbs: *increasingly popular*, *increasingly difficult*, *increasingly common*. It describes a trend, so it often comes with *become* or *get* (*is becoming increasingly …*). It can also start a sentence: *Increasingly, people work from home*.
entries.pattern: increasingly + adjective; become / get increasingly + adjective; Increasingly, …
examples: Electric bikes are becoming **increasingly** popular with commuters.
As the night went on, the guests got **increasingly** loud.
**Increasingly**, patients book their appointments online.

drill.sentence: As the deadline got closer, my roommate became {{increasingly}} stressed and stopped sleeping.
drill.hint: -ly adverb: to a growing degree (not *progressively*)

entries.related: *more and more* — conversational; *progressively* — step by step, formal; *gradually* — slowly over time.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: For this reason; that is why. It introduces a result that follows from what was just said.
entries.usage: Mainly in formal and academic writing; in speech it sounds stiff, so people say *so* or *that's why*. It is often followed directly by a noun phrase with no verb (*The roads were icy; hence the delay*). Careful writers don't join two full clauses with only a comma and *hence*; use a semicolon or *and hence*.
entries.pattern: …, hence + noun phrase; …; hence + clause; and hence
examples: The bakery only uses local organic flour, **hence** the higher prices.
Many rural hospitals can't find enough nurses, and **hence** some have stopped delivering babies.
She grew up in Texas; **hence** her strong opinions about barbecue.

drill.sentence: The restaurant is run by a family from Naples, {{hence}} the excellent pizza.
drill.hint: one formal adverb meaning *for this reason* (not *thus*)

entries.related: *therefore* — formal, before a clause; *thus* — formal, as a result; *that's why* — conversational.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Real and exactly what it seems to be, not fake; or, of feelings and people, sincere and honest.
entries.usage: Common in everyday speech and writing: *genuine leather*, *genuine interest*, *a genuine concern*, *a genuine person*. About people and feelings, it is warm praise (*She's really genuine*). Most Americans say JEN-yoo-in; *JEN-yoo-wine* is heard in some regions but sounds nonstandard to many speakers.
entries.pattern: genuine + leather / interest / concern; a genuine person
examples: Is this bag **genuine** leather, or is it fake?
Her surprise looked **genuine**; I don't think she knew about the party.
He's one of the most **genuine** people I know; what you see is what you get.

drill.sentence: The jeweler confirmed that the diamond in my grandmother's ring was {{genuine}}, not glass.
drill.hint: adjective: the real thing (not *real* or *authentic*)

entries.related: *authentic* — truly from its claimed origin; *sincere* — honest in feelings; *fake* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Something that a person, event or period leaves behind for later generations, such as achievements, influence or problems.
entries.usage: Common in the news, sports and business: *leave a legacy*, *her legacy as a teacher*, *the legacy of the war*. It can be positive or negative. In tech, *legacy* as an adjective means old but still in use (*legacy systems*), often with a hint of complaint.
entries.pattern: leave a legacy; someone's legacy as + role; the legacy of + event
examples: The coach's real **legacy** is the hundreds of kids he taught to love the game.
The factory closed decades ago, but its **legacy** of polluted soil remains.
We still have to support a **legacy** system that was written in the 1990s.

drill.sentence: My grandfather wanted to leave a {{legacy}}, so he gave his land to the town for a public park.
drill.hint: noun: something that lasts for future generations (not *mark* or *gift*)

entries.related: *heritage* — traditions and culture passed down; *inheritance* — money or property left to someone; *leave your mark* — have a lasting influence.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Only, and nothing more; used to show that something is small or less important than people might think.
entries.usage: Common in writing and careful speech: *I was merely asking*, *merely a suggestion*, *not merely X but Y*. It often defends or downplays something (*I'm merely pointing out …*), so it can sound slightly defensive or formal. In casual speech, *just* is more natural.
entries.pattern: merely + verb / noun phrase; not merely X but (also) Y
examples: I'm not criticizing you; I'm **merely** pointing out that we're over budget.
The scratch on the car is **merely** cosmetic, so it doesn't affect safety.
For her, running isn't **merely** exercise; it's how she clears her head.

drill.sentence: Don't get upset; it was {{merely}} a suggestion, and you're free to ignore it.
drill.hint: adverb: nothing more than (formal; not *just*, *only* or *simply*)

entries.related: *just* — conversational; *simply* — only, or in a simple way; *mere* — the adjective (*a mere five minutes*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Complete, and including everything or nearly everything that is needed or relevant.
entries.usage: Common in formal writing, business, health and insurance: *a comprehensive review*, *a comprehensive guide*, *comprehensive coverage*. It suggests thoroughness and often appears in titles and marketing. Don't confuse it with *comprehensible*, which means easy to understand.
entries.pattern: a comprehensive + review / guide / plan / list / approach
examples: The book is a **comprehensive** guide to hiking in Colorado, with maps of over two hundred trails.
Our car insurance includes **comprehensive** coverage, so the hail damage was paid for.
The hospital is doing a **comprehensive** review of its safety procedures.

drill.sentence: Before you buy an old house, get a {{comprehensive}} inspection that covers the roof, the wiring and the plumbing.
drill.hint: adjective: covering everything (not *thorough*, *full*, *detailed* or *complete*)

entries.related: *thorough* — careful and detailed; *exhaustive* — covering every possible detail; *comprehensible* — easy to understand, a different word.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Based on facts and evidence, not influenced by personal feelings, opinions or interests.
entries.usage: Common in journalism, science, law and work evaluations: *an objective assessment*, *objective evidence*, *try to be objective*. It is often used about people who must judge fairly (*I can't be objective; she's my daughter*). The opposite is *subjective*, and the noun is *objectivity*.
entries.pattern: be / stay objective (about something); objective + evidence / criteria / assessment
examples: It's hard to be **objective** about your own kid's singing.
Judges are supposed to be **objective**, but even they have bad days.
We need **objective** data on traffic before we install a stoplight.

drill.sentence: I asked a friend who doesn't know my boyfriend for an {{objective}} opinion on our fight.
drill.hint: adjective: not influenced by personal feelings (not *unbiased*, *impartial*, *independent*, *honest* or *outside*)

entries.related: *impartial* — not favoring either side; *unbiased* — without prejudice; *subjective* — based on personal feelings.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A new plan or program to solve a problem or reach a goal; also the ability to act and make decisions without being told.
entries.usage: Common in business, government and schools: *launch an initiative*, *a new initiative to reduce waste*. In the second sense it is uncountable and usually praise: *show initiative*, *take the initiative*, *on your own initiative*. Employers often say they want people who *take initiative*.
entries.pattern: launch / announce an initiative (to + verb); show / take (the) initiative
examples: The city launched a new **initiative** to plant ten thousand trees by 2030.
Nobody asked her to fix the schedule; she did it on her own **initiative**.
In my review, my manager said I need to show more **initiative** in meetings.

drill.sentence: The new intern showed real {{initiative}}: she noticed the broken printer and called the repair company herself.
drill.hint: noun: the ability to act without being told (not *drive* or *leadership*)

entries.related: *a program* — an organized plan of activities; *a campaign* — planned actions to reach a goal; *drive* — strong motivation.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Approximately; not exactly (*roughly 20 people*).
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing before numbers, amounts and times: *roughly half*, *roughly ten minutes*, *roughly the same size*. It sounds more natural in speech than *approximately*, and *roughly speaking* means *in general terms*. With verbs, it has a different sense: violently or without care (*handle the box roughly*).
entries.pattern: roughly + number / half / the same; roughly speaking
examples: **Roughly** twenty people came to the neighborhood meeting.
The drive from Denver to Aspen takes **roughly** four hours.
The two apartments are **roughly** the same size, but one has a much better view.

drill.sentence: The trip will cost {{roughly}} two thousand dollars, including flights and hotels.
drill.hint: adverb: not exactly (not *about*, *around* or *approximately*)

entries.related: *about* / *around* — conversational; *approximately* — formal; *exactly* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To show or suggest that something is true or exists, usually without proving it.
entries.usage: Common in research, the news, medicine and forms: *Studies indicate that …*, *these symptoms indicate …*, *indicate your choice*. It sounds more formal than *show* and weaker than *prove*. On forms, it means *state* or *mark* (*Please indicate your size*).
entries.pattern: indicate (that) + clause; indicate + a problem / interest; please indicate + choice
examples: Early surveys **indicate** that most residents want a dog park.
A fever and a stiff neck can **indicate** a serious infection, so call a doctor.
Please **indicate** your shirt size on the registration form.

drill.sentence: Dark clouds over the mountains usually {{indicate}} that a storm is coming.
drill.hint: verb: are a sign (not *mean*, *suggest*, *signal* or *show*)

entries.related: *suggest* — point to something without proof, softer; *show* — make clear; *signal* — be a sign of, or make a sign.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: The final result of an action, process, event or situation.
entries.usage: Common in formal speech and writing, especially in medicine, law, sports and research: *the outcome of the trial*, *patient outcomes*, *a positive outcome*. It is more formal than *result* and is often used when the result was uncertain. It is usually followed by *of*.
entries.pattern: the outcome of + event; a positive / likely / possible outcome; patient outcomes
examples: Whatever the **outcome** of the trial, the family wants the truth to come out.
The doctors are hopeful about the **outcome** of the surgery.
We were happy with the **outcome**: the landlord agreed to fix the heating and lower the rent.

drill.sentence: Both teams played well, but the {{outcome}} of the game wasn't decided until the last second.
drill.hint: noun: how it ended up (not *result* or *winner*)

entries.related: *result* — more general and conversational; *consequence* — an effect, often negative; *output* — what a machine or person produces.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To give money, time, ideas or effort to something shared; or to be one of the causes of a result.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in the news and in everyday life: *contribute to a project*, *contribute twenty dollars to a gift*, *contribute to climate change*. In the cause sense, it suggests one factor among several, so it is more careful than *cause*. Americans stress the second syllable; *CON-tri-bute* is mainly British.
entries.pattern: contribute + money / ideas + to something; contribute to + a problem / result
examples: Everyone in the office **contributed** twenty dollars to Maria's farewell gift.
Poor sleep can **contribute to** weight gain and high blood pressure.
She **contributed** a lot of good ideas in her first month on the team.

drill.sentence: The heavy rain {{contributed to}} the accident, but the main cause was speeding.
drill.hint: verb + preposition: was one of the causes of (not *led to* or *added to*)

entries.related: *cause* — be the main reason; *donate* — give money or goods to a cause; *play a role in* — be one factor.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Large in amount, value or importance.
entries.usage: Common at work, in the news and in finance: *a substantial amount*, *a substantial increase*, *substantial evidence*, *a substantial meal*. It sounds more formal and serious than *big* or *a lot of*. Don't confuse it with *substantive*, which means dealing with real, important issues (*substantive changes*).
entries.pattern: a substantial + amount / increase / sum / raise; substantial evidence
examples: The new job comes with a **substantial** raise, so we can finally afford a bigger apartment.
Our neighbors spent a **substantial** sum on repairing the roof after the storm.
There is **substantial** evidence that regular exercise improves mood.

drill.sentence: We put down a {{substantial}} deposit on the house, so we really don't want to lose it.
drill.hint: adjective: large and serious (formal; not *large*, *sizable*, *hefty* or *considerable*)

entries.related: *considerable* — large, very close; *significant* — large or important enough to matter; *substantive* — about real issues.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Basic and most important, forming the base on which other things depend.
entries.usage: Common in serious discussion, law, science and education: *a fundamental change*, *a fundamental right*, *be fundamental to something*. It stresses depth: a *fundamental problem* cannot be fixed with small changes. The noun *the fundamentals* means the basic skills or facts (*the fundamentals of cooking*).
entries.pattern: a fundamental + change / problem / right / difference; be fundamental to something
examples: The new manager wants to make **fundamental** changes to how the store is run, not just put up a new sign.
There's a **fundamental** difference between being alone and being lonely.
Trust is **fundamental** to any good relationship.

drill.sentence: The team keeps losing because of a {{fundamental}} problem: the players don't talk to each other.
drill.hint: adjective: at the very base of everything (not *basic*, *core* or *serious*)

entries.related: *basic* — simple and necessary; *essential* — absolutely necessary; *underlying* — hidden but causing the visible problem.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Well known and important; or easy to see because it is large or stands out.
entries.usage: Common in the news, business and descriptions: *a prominent lawyer*, *a prominent figure in*, *play a prominent role*, *a prominent nose*. For people, it means respected and influential, not necessarily famous everywhere. For things, *display something prominently* means put it where people will notice it.
entries.pattern: a prominent + figure / lawyer / member / role; feature prominently
examples: A **prominent** local surgeon donated a million dollars to the children's hospital.
The new library has a **prominent** spot on Main Street, right across from City Hall.
Restaurants have to show calorie counts in a **prominent** place on the menu.

drill.sentence: Her father was a {{prominent}} lawyer in Atlanta, so everyone in town knew the family.
drill.hint: adjective: important and widely known in the community (not *famous*, *well-known*, *respected* or *powerful*)

mistake.wrong: Lots of prominents came to the premiere.
mistake.right: Lots of celebrities came to the premiere.
mistake.why: *Prominent* is only an adjective; for famous people as a group, say *celebrities*, not German-style *Prominente*.

entries.related: *well-known* — known by many people; *eminent* — famous and respected in a profession, formal; *conspicuous* — very easy to see, often in a bad way.
